definition: a pause or gap in something that is otherwise continuous

examples.text: After a ten-year hiatus, the games were held again in 1896.
The fossil record shows a hiatus of several million years at this site.
The band is back after a two-year hiatus, and tickets sold out in minutes.

confused.note: A hiatus is a neutral pause; a lapse is a slip or a failure.

questions.passage: The magazine did not close for good in 1975. After a ______ of nearly a decade, during which its editors pursued other projects, it resumed publication with a new design and many of its original writers.
questions.explanation: A decade-long pause before resuming is a gap in something continuous.

distractors.why: A debacle is a complete failure, which a pause followed by a successful return is not.
A modicum is a small amount, which does not fit "of nearly a decade."
An anecdote is a short personal story, which does not describe a break in publication.

definition: easy to see or notice; attracting attention

examples.text: The male bird's conspicuous red crest makes it easy to spot.
The general was conspicuous on the field in his white coat.
I felt conspicuous as the only person at the party in a costume.

confused.note: Conspicuous means easy to notice; suspicious means distrustful or arousing distrust.

questions.passage: Most moths in the forest are brown or gray and nearly invisible against bark. The tiger moth is a ______ exception: its orange wings can be seen from across a clearing, a warning to birds that it tastes foul.
questions.explanation: Wings visible from across a clearing are easy to notice.

distractors.why: Oblivious means unaware, which does not describe a visible moth.
Sedentary means staying in one place, which is not the contrast with invisible moths.
Hapless means unlucky, which does not fit a moth protected by its warning color.

definition: not aware of what is happening around you

examples.text: Oblivious to the storm outside, the scholar reads on by candlelight.
The court danced on, oblivious to the army gathering at the border.
With headphones on, he was oblivious to the fire drill.

confused.note: Oblivious means unaware; obvious means easy to see.

questions.passage: The chess players were so absorbed in their game that they remained ______ to everything else. Neither noticed when the café lights were dimmed, the chairs stacked, or the door locked behind the last waiter.
questions.explanation: Not noticing the café closing around them shows they were unaware.

distractors.why: Vigilant means watchful, the opposite of noticing nothing.
Conspicuous means easy to see, which does not complete "to everything else."
Palatable means pleasant to taste or accept, which does not fit.

definition: done or shown openly, not hidden

examples.text: The duke avoided any overt act of rebellion while quietly arming his castles.
The disease can spread before a patient shows overt symptoms.
There was no overt hostility at dinner, just a lot of very polite silence.

confused.note: Overt means open; covert means hidden. They are opposites.

questions.passage: The company never issued a direct threat to employees who spoke with reporters. Its methods were less ______: those who gave interviews found that their requests for leave were delayed and their projects quietly reassigned.
questions.explanation: Delays and reassignments are hidden pressure, less open than a direct threat.

distractors.why: Covert means hidden; "less covert" would mean more open, the reverse of what is described.
Deft means skillful, which is not the contrast with a direct threat.
Culpable means deserving blame; the sentence contrasts open and hidden methods.

definition: enthusiastic public praise

examples.text: Her first collection of stories won wide acclaim from critics.
The engineer returned home to public acclaim after the canal opened.
My chili recipe earned acclaim at the neighborhood cook-off.

confused.note: Acclaim is praise; to acclimate is to get used to a new climate or situation.

questions.passage: The documentary was shown in only a handful of theaters and earned little money. It did, however, receive considerable ______: three major critics named it the best film of the year.
questions.explanation: Being named best film by critics is enthusiastic praise.

distractors.why: Animosity is hostility, the opposite of critics' praise.
A hiatus is a pause, which a film cannot receive.
A modicum is a small amount and needs "of something"; it cannot stand alone here.

partsNote: from Latin clamare, "to shout": shouting toward

definition: very different from each other; made up of unlike things

examples.text: The study combines data from disparate fields, including geology and economics.
The empire united disparate peoples under a single code of law.
My friends have disparate tastes, so choosing a movie takes an hour.

confused.note: Disparate means very different; desperate means without hope or in great need.

questions.passage: The orchestra's new director has brought together musicians from ______ traditions. A jazz drummer, a classical harpist, and a player of the Malian kora now rehearse side by side.
questions.explanation: Jazz, classical, and Malian music are very different traditions.

distractors.why: Homogeneous means all of the same kind, the opposite of this group.
Redundant means needlessly repeated, which varied traditions are not.
Desperate means in great need; it only looks like the right word.

partsNote: from Latin parare, "to prepare, to arrange": set apart

definition: a short, interesting story about a real person or event

examples.text: The biography opens with an anecdote about the president's first job.
An anecdote about one patient is not evidence that a treatment works.
My uncle has an anecdote for every occasion, most involving fish.

confused.note: An anecdote is a short story; an antidote is a cure for poison.

questions.passage: The speaker began not with statistics but with an ______. She described the afternoon her grandmother, then eighty, decided to learn to swim, and the audience was hers from that moment on.
questions.explanation: A short personal story about her grandmother is an anecdote.

distractors.why: An antidote is a remedy for poison; it sounds similar but does not fit.
An accolade is an honor, not a way to begin a speech.
A hiatus is a pause, which does not describe a story.

definition: a strong feeling of dislike or hatred

examples.text: Decades of animosity between the two cities ended with a shared railway.
The brothers' animosity dates from a quarrel over their father's will.
There is no real animosity between our schools, just a loud football rivalry.

confused.note: Animosity is hostility; animation is liveliness.

questions.passage: The two candidates had exchanged bitter insults throughout the campaign. Their ______ was still evident on election night, when the loser declined the customary telephone call to congratulate the winner.
questions.explanation: Refusing even a customary courtesy shows lingering hostility.

distractors.why: Acclaim is praise, which neither candidate offered.
A complement completes something else, which does not describe their feelings.
Deference means respectful yielding, the opposite of this snub.

partsNote: from Latin animus, "spirit," in the sense of angry spirit

definition: impressively great in size, amount, or ability

examples.text: The whale consumes a prodigious quantity of krill each day.
Building the pyramid required a prodigious effort from thousands of workers.
My brother has a prodigious appetite and can finish a whole pizza alone.

confused.note: Prodigious means impressively large or great; prodigal means wasteful.

questions.passage: The composer's output was ______. In a career of only twenty years he wrote more than a thousand works, among them forty operas and enough church music to fill a concert season.
questions.explanation: More than a thousand works in twenty years is impressively large.

distractors.why: Meager means small in amount, the opposite of his output.
Prodigal means wasteful; it resembles the right word but means something else.
Sedentary means involving much sitting, which does not describe output.

definition: deserving blame for something bad

examples.text: The inquiry found the captain culpable for sailing without enough lifeboats.
The narrator feels culpable for a death he could not have prevented.
I am at least partly culpable for the empty cookie jar.

confused.note: Culpable means blameworthy; capable means able.

questions.passage: Investigators concluded that the bridge's collapse was not an unavoidable accident. The firm that built it was ______, they found, having ignored two engineers' warnings that the steel was too thin.
questions.explanation: Ignoring warnings makes the firm deserving of blame.

distractors.why: Hapless means unlucky; the firm was at fault, not merely unfortunate.
Inviolable means never to be broken, which does not describe a firm.
Bereft means deprived of something, which does not fit.

definition: completely lacking something, or sad because of a loss

examples.text: Bereft of friends in the new city, the heroine writes long letters home.
The retreating army was bereft of food, maps, and hope.
When my phone died on the trip, I felt strangely bereft.

confused.note: Bereft means lacking or deprived of anything; bereaved means having lost a loved one to death.

questions.passage: After the mill closed, the town was ______ of its only large employer. Shops along the main street shut one after another, and within five years a third of the houses stood empty.
questions.explanation: The town was deprived of its main employer.

distractors.why: Replete means full of, the opposite of losing something.
Oblivious means unaware of, which does not describe losing an employer.
Culpable means deserving blame, which does not fit "of its only large employer."

definition: to give or do something in return for something similar

examples.text: The king sent a gift of horses, and the emperor reciprocated with silk.
The plants supply sugar to the fungus, which reciprocates with minerals.
She invited me to her party, so I reciprocated with an invitation to mine.

confused.note: Reciprocate is the verb; reciprocal is the adjective meaning given in return.

questions.passage: When a neighbor shoveled her driveway after the storm, Ms. Odum wanted to ______ the kindness. The following week she left a loaf of warm bread on his porch.
questions.explanation: Leaving bread in return for shoveling is repaying a kindness.

distractors.why: Chastise means to scold, which one does not do to a kindness.
Debunk means to expose as false, which does not fit.
Proscribe means to forbid, which is not her intent.

definition: to criticize or scold someone severely

examples.text: The pamphlet chastised the council for neglecting the city's wells.
The governess chastises the children for tracking mud across the hall.
Dad chastised me for leaving the freezer door open all night.

confused.note: Chastise means to scold; chaste means pure or simple in style.

questions.passage: The coach was not one to shout during a game. Afterward, though, she would ______ any player who had ignored the team's plan, explaining in detail exactly how the lapse had hurt the others.
questions.explanation: Explaining how a lapse hurt the team is a firm scolding.

distractors.why: Acclaim means to praise, the opposite of scolding.
Satiate means to satisfy fully, which does not fit.
Reciprocate means to return a favor, which is not what the coach does.

definition: never to be broken, harmed, or dishonored

examples.text: The ambassadors were promised inviolable safe passage through enemy lands.
To the old sailor, a promise made at sea is inviolable.
Sunday dinner with the whole family is an inviolable tradition at our house.

confused.note: Inviolable means never to be broken; invaluable means extremely useful or precious.

questions.passage: The scientists regarded one rule as ______: no result would be announced until a second team had repeated the experiment. Even under pressure from sponsors, they never made an exception.
questions.explanation: A rule never broken even under pressure is treated as unbreakable.

distractors.why: Redundant means unnecessary, which is not how they regarded the rule.
Palatable means agreeable, which does not capture a rule that is never broken.
Overt means done openly, which is not the quality described.

definition: to satisfy a need or desire completely

examples.text: A single large meal can satiate a python for weeks.
No amount of gold could satiate the dragon's greed.
Three tacos finally satiated my hunger after practice.

confused.note: To satiate is to satisfy fully; to saturate is to soak completely.

questions.passage: The first volume of the diaries only increased readers' curiosity about the reclusive author. Publishers hope that the second, which covers the years of her greatest fame, will finally ______ it.
questions.explanation: The second volume is expected to satisfy the readers' curiosity.

distractors.why: Instigate means to stir up, but curiosity already exists and is to be satisfied.
Castigate means to criticize harshly, which does not fit curiosity.
Usurp means to seize power wrongfully, which does not fit.

definition: to criticize or punish someone severely

examples.text: The senator castigated the navy for losing three ships in one month.
The critic castigates the author for wasting a brilliant premise.
The referee castigated both captains for the brawl.

confused.note: Castigate means to criticize harshly; instigate means to start or stir up.

questions.passage: The inspector's report did more than note a few problems. It ______ the hospital's managers, describing their record keeping as "a disgrace" and their response to complaints as "contemptuous."
questions.explanation: Calling the managers' work a disgrace is severe criticism.

distractors.why: Exonerated means cleared of blame, the opposite of this report.
Instigated means provoked or started something; it resembles the right word but does not mean criticized.
Reciprocated means gave in return, which does not fit.

definition: to forbid something officially

examples.text: The new regime proscribed all newspapers that had supported the old king.
The treaty proscribes the testing of weapons in outer space.
School rules proscribe phones in the exam room.

confused.note: Proscribe means to forbid; prescribe means to order or recommend. They are nearly opposites.

questions.passage: Far from encouraging the practice, the medical board has ______ it. Any physician who continues to prescribe the drug for children now risks losing the license to practice.
questions.explanation: A penalty for continuing shows the board has forbidden the practice.

distractors.why: Prescribed means recommended or ordered, nearly the opposite of forbidden.
Facilitated means made easier, which the first clause rules out.
Reciprocated means returned in kind, which does not fit.

partsNote: to write publicly, to post a ban

definition: involving a lot of sitting and little physical activity; staying in one place

examples.text: A sedentary lifestyle raises the risk of heart disease.
Farming turned wandering bands into sedentary villagers.
After a sedentary week of exams, I needed a long run.

confused.note: Sedentary means sitting or settled; sedimentary describes rock formed from settled layers.

questions.passage: Office work is largely ______. Doctors therefore advise employees who spend eight hours at a desk to stand and stretch every hour and to walk during lunch.
questions.explanation: Eight hours at a desk involves much sitting and little movement.

distractors.why: Strenuous means requiring great physical effort, the opposite of desk work.
Futile means pointless, which is not what the advice addresses.
Hapless means unlucky, which does not describe office work.

definition: pleasant to taste, or acceptable to the mind

examples.text: Sugar was added to make the bitter medicine more palatable to children.
The minister softened the treaty's wording to make it palatable to parliament.
A little cheese makes broccoli far more palatable to my brother.

confused.note: Palatable means pleasant or acceptable; palpable means able to be felt.

questions.passage: Voters rejected the first proposal, which would have doubled parking fees overnight. The council then offered a more ______ version, raising fees by a small amount each year over a decade.
questions.explanation: A gradual increase is easier for voters to accept.

distractors.why: Onerous means burdensome, the opposite of a version meant to be easier to accept.
Conspicuous means easy to notice, which is not what made the new version succeed.
Culpable means blameworthy, which does not describe a proposal.

partsNote: from "palate," the roof of the mouth

definition: unlucky and deserving sympathy

examples.text: The hapless clerk loses his hat, his job, and his train ticket in a single chapter.
The hapless expedition ran aground twice before leaving the harbor.
A hapless tourist stood in the rain, holding a map upside down.

confused.note: Hapless means unlucky; helpless means unable to help oneself.

questions.passage: The comedy follows a ______ traveler for whom nothing goes right. His luggage is sent to the wrong continent, his hotel has no record of him, and the one taxi he finds runs out of fuel a mile from the airport.
questions.explanation: A traveler for whom everything goes wrong is unlucky.

distractors.why: Deft means skillful, which does not describe someone overwhelmed by bad luck.
Culpable means blameworthy, but his troubles are bad luck, not his fault.
Prodigious means impressively great, which does not fit.

definition: quick and skillful

examples.text: With a few deft strokes of the pen, the cartoonist summed up the scandal.
The pickpocket's deft fingers are in and out of the coat before the owner blinks.
She flipped the pancake with a deft twist of the wrist.

confused.note: Deft means skillful; daft is an informal word for silly.

questions.passage: Spectators marveled at the potter's ______ hands. In under a minute, and with what looked like no effort at all, she drew a shapeless lump of clay up into a tall, perfectly even vase.
questions.explanation: Shaping a perfect vase quickly and easily shows skill.

distractors.why: Inept means clumsy, the opposite of her hands.
Sedentary means involving sitting, which does not describe skillful hands.
Bereft means deprived, which does not fit.

definition: to show that a belief or claim is false

examples.text: The study debunked the idea that sugar makes children hyperactive.
Historians have debunked the legend that the emperor fiddled while the city burned.
A quick search debunked my brother's claim that goldfish have three-second memories.

confused.note: To debunk is to expose a false claim; to debug is to fix errors in a program.

questions.passage: For years, a popular website claimed that people use only a tenth of their brains. Neuroscientists have thoroughly ______ this myth, showing with scans that nearly every region is active over the course of a day.
questions.explanation: Brain scans show the claim is false.

distractors.why: Promulgated means spread or announced, the opposite of disproving the myth.
Satiated means fully satisfied, which does not fit a myth.
Usurped means seized wrongfully, which does not fit.

definition: to make an action or process easier

examples.text: Enzymes facilitate chemical reactions that would otherwise take years.
Paved roads facilitated trade between the coast and the interior.
A shared calendar facilitates planning when five people use one car.

confused.note: Facilitate means to make easier; felicitate means to congratulate.

questions.passage: The new footbridge was built to ______ travel between the two halves of the campus. Students who once walked twenty minutes around the ravine can now cross it in two.
questions.explanation: Cutting a twenty-minute walk to two makes travel easier.

distractors.why: Proscribe means to forbid, the opposite of helping students cross.
Debunk means to expose as false, which does not fit travel.
Chastise means to scold, which makes no sense here.

definition: existing as a natural and permanent part of something

examples.text: There is an inherent uncertainty in any measurement.
The founders believed in rights inherent in every person.
There is an inherent risk in lending your bike to my brother.

confused.note: Inherent means built in by nature; to inherit is to receive from a parent or predecessor.

questions.passage: The danger is not a flaw in this particular reactor design. It is ______ in the technology itself: any plant that uses the fuel must store waste that stays hazardous for thousands of years.
questions.explanation: A danger found in every plant using the fuel is built into the technology.

distractors.why: Extraneous means coming from outside or irrelevant, the opposite of built in.
Palatable means acceptable, which does not fit a danger "in the technology itself."
Hapless means unlucky, which does not fit.

partsNote: from Latin haerere, "to stick": sticking in

definition: to add to something in a way that improves it or makes it complete

examples.text: Field observations complement the data collected by satellite.
The spare illustrations complement the poems without competing with them.
The tart lemon sauce complements the sweetness of the cake.

confused.note: To complement is to complete or go well with; to compliment is to praise.

questions.passage: The two founders succeeded partly because their abilities ______ each other. One was a gifted engineer with no patience for customers; the other could sell anything but could not read a blueprint.
questions.explanation: Each founder supplied what the other lacked, completing the partnership.

distractors.why: Complimented means praised; the point is that their skills fit together.
Duplicated means copied exactly, but their abilities were different.
Castigated means criticized harshly, which abilities cannot do.

partsNote: from Latin plere, "to fill": to fill up

definition: not needed because something else already does the same thing; repeating

examples.text: The spacecraft carries redundant computers so that one failure cannot end the mission.
"Free gift" is redundant, since every gift is free.
Saying "ATM machine" is redundant because the M already stands for machine.

confused.note: Redundant means unnecessary because it duplicates something; repetitive simply means repeated many times.

questions.passage: The editor struck the phrase "in my personal opinion" wherever it appeared. It was ______, she explained: an opinion is always personal, and the essay's first line had already made clear whose views it contained.
questions.explanation: The phrase repeats what is already known, so it is unnecessary.

distractors.why: Pristine means fresh and unspoiled, which does not describe a needless phrase.
Vicarious means experienced through someone else, which does not fit.
Tenacious means persistent, which does not explain why the phrase was cut.

definition: lower in rank or importance

examples.text: Subordinate officers were forbidden to question the general's orders.
In the wolf pack, subordinate animals eat after the leaders.
On the group project, I happily took a subordinate role and made the slides.

confused.note: Subordinate means lower in rank; insubordinate means refusing to obey.

questions.passage: In the artist's early murals, landscape plays a ______ role, serving only as a backdrop for the human figures. In her late work the relationship is reversed, and tiny people are dwarfed by mountains.
questions.explanation: A backdrop that serves the figures is of lower importance.

distractors.why: Dominant means most important, which describes landscape in her late work.
Apocryphal means of doubtful truth, which does not describe a role in a painting.
Lethargic means sluggish, which does not fit.

definition: willing to do what others ask or what rules require

examples.text: A compliant parliament approved every law the king proposed.
The new engines are compliant with the stricter emission standards.
Our usually stubborn dog was oddly compliant at the vet.

confused.note: Compliant means obedient; a complaint is an expression of unhappiness.

questions.passage: Inspectors found that only one of the forty restaurants was fully ______ with the new hygiene code. The rest had failed to install the required sinks or to keep the temperature records the law demands.
questions.explanation: Meeting the code's requirements is following the rules.

distractors.why: Obsequious means fawning and overeager to please, the wrong tone for meeting a legal standard.
Vigilant means watchful, and it does not fit "with the new hygiene code."
Futile means pointless, which does not fit.

definition: very generous, rich, or expensive; more than enough

examples.text: The emperor held a lavish banquet with a thousand dishes.
The critic was lavish in her praise of the young poet.
My aunt throws lavish birthday parties, complete with a chocolate fountain.

confused.note: Lavish means generous or luxurious; ravish means to seize or to delight intensely.

questions.passage: The premiere was a ______ affair. Guests arrived by horse-drawn carriage, dined on lobster beneath crystal chandeliers, and each went home with a silver box engraved with the film's title.
questions.explanation: Carriages, lobster, and silver gifts describe a rich, expensive event.

distractors.why: Pristine means spotless and unspoiled; the passage stresses expense and luxury.
Docile means easily managed, which does not describe an event.
Pernicious means harmful, which is not suggested.

definition: having no chance of success; pointless

examples.text: After the walls fell, further resistance was futile.
Attempts to stop the leak with tape proved futile.
Arguing with a toddler about bedtime is futile.

confused.note: Futile means pointless; feudal relates to the medieval system of lords and vassals.

questions.passage: Rescuers searched the mountainside through the night, but their efforts were ______. Fresh snow had buried every track, and by dawn it was clear that the lost hikers could not be found on foot.
questions.explanation: A search that could not succeed was pointless.

distractors.why: Lavish means rich and generous, which does not describe a failed search.
Tenacious means persistent; the efforts may have been persistent, but "but" signals that they failed.
Compliant means obedient, which does not fit.

definition: not supporting any side; fair

examples.text: Both nations agreed to let an impartial judge draw the border.
A good experiment needs impartial observers who do not know which group got the drug.
I cannot be impartial about pizza toppings; pineapple is simply wrong.

confused.note: Impartial means fair to all sides; impassive means showing no emotion.

questions.passage: Because both companies had hired her in the past, the engineer doubted that she could be ______. She therefore declined to serve as referee in their dispute and suggested someone with no ties to either.
questions.explanation: Ties to both companies might keep her from judging fairly.

distractors.why: Vigilant means watchful, which is not the quality a referee with past ties might lack.
Mercurial means quick to change mood, which is not her worry.
Reclusive means avoiding company, which is unrelated.

partsNote: not taking a part or side

definition: watching carefully for danger or problems

examples.text: Vigilant sentries spotted the fire ships before they reached the harbor.
Meerkats take turns standing vigilant while the rest of the group feeds.
Be vigilant about emails asking for your password.

confused.note: Vigilant means watchful; a vigilante is a person who enforces the law without authority.

questions.passage: Lifeguards at the beach must remain ______ throughout their shifts. A swimmer in trouble may slip under the surface in seconds, so guards are trained never to look away from the water for longer than it takes to blink.
questions.explanation: Never looking away from the water is watching carefully for danger.

distractors.why: Lethargic means sluggish and drowsy, the opposite of what a lifeguard must be.
Docile means easily led, which is not the quality required.
Impartial means unbiased, which is not what watching swimmers requires.

definition: in perfect condition, as if new; clean and unspoiled

examples.text: The lake's pristine water supports species found nowhere else.
The tomb was found in pristine condition, sealed for three thousand years.
My sister keeps her sneakers pristine and never wears them in the rain.

confused.note: Pristine means unspoiled; primitive means at an early, simple stage.

questions.passage: The valley has no roads, and the only way in is a two-day walk over a high pass. As a result it remains ______, its forests uncut and its river so clear that fish can be counted from the bank.
questions.explanation: Uncut forests and a clear river describe an unspoiled place.

distractors.why: Convoluted means overly complicated, which does not describe a valley.
Redundant means unnecessary, which does not fit.
Subordinate means lower in rank, which does not fit.

definition: a sudden and complete failure, often an embarrassing one

examples.text: The invasion was a debacle that cost the general his command.
The dinner party ends in debacle when the soufflé explodes.
The school play was a debacle: the set fell over in the first act.

confused.note: A debacle is a disastrous failure; a debate is a formal argument.

questions.passage: The product launch was a ______. The website crashed within minutes, the first shipment contained the wrong parts, and the chief executive's microphone failed during her televised announcement.
questions.explanation: A crashed site, wrong parts, and a failed microphone add up to an embarrassing failure.

distractors.why: A triumph is a great success, the opposite of this launch.
A modicum is a small amount, which does not describe an event.
A hiatus is a pause, which is not what the passage describes.

definition: extremely complicated and hard to follow

examples.text: The mystery's convoluted plot involves three stolen identities and a forged map.
The convoluted treaty required forty pages to define a single border.
His convoluted directions sent us through four neighborhoods to reach a store two blocks away.

confused.note: Convoluted means tangled and complicated; convulsed means shaken violently.

questions.passage: The tax form's instructions are needlessly ______. To learn whether a single deduction applies, a reader must consult page three, which refers to a table on page nine, which in turn depends on a definition in a separate booklet.
questions.explanation: Instructions that send readers through page after page are complicated and hard to follow.

distractors.why: Pristine means clean and unspoiled, which does not describe tangled instructions.
Futile means pointless; the instructions can be followed, but only with difficulty.
Docile means easily managed, which does not fit.

definition: not giving up easily; holding firmly

examples.text: The tenacious defenders held the pass for a week.
The plant's tenacious roots grip bare rock.
My tenacious little sister asked for a puppy every day for two years, and it worked.

confused.note: Tenacious means holding on firmly; tenuous means weak or thin.

questions.passage: The reporter was nothing if not ______. Denied an interview eleven times, she kept writing, telephoning, and waiting outside the minister's office until, on the twelfth attempt, he agreed to speak with her.
questions.explanation: Trying twelve times without giving up shows persistence.

distractors.why: Lethargic means sluggish, the opposite of her energy.
Mercurial means changeable, but she never changed course.
Impartial means unbiased, which is not the trait shown.

definition: to rise and fall or change often and irregularly

examples.text: The animal's body temperature fluctuates with the air around it.
The price of bread fluctuated wildly during the siege.
My interest in jogging fluctuates with the weather.

confused.note: Things fluctuate; people who cannot decide vacillate.

questions.passage: The lake's level does not stay constant. It ______ with the seasons, rising as much as three meters during the spring melt and falling again through the dry months of late summer.
questions.explanation: Rising in spring and falling in summer is going up and down.

distractors.why: Stagnates means stops moving or changing, which the first sentence rules out.
Flouts means openly disobeys a rule, which does not fit a lake.
Usurps means seizes power wrongfully, which does not fit.

definition: quiet and easy to control or teach

examples.text: Centuries of breeding turned wild cattle into docile farm animals.
The docile pupil never once questions the schoolmaster.
Our docile old dog lets the baby tug his ears.

confused.note: Docile means easily managed; ductile describes metal that can be drawn into wire.

questions.passage: First-time riders are given the stable's most ______ horse. She walks at an even pace, stops at the slightest pull of the reins, and has never been known to bolt, even when startled.
questions.explanation: A horse that responds gently and never bolts is easy to control.

distractors.why: Mercurial means unpredictable, the opposite of this steady horse.
Tenacious means persistent, which is not what a beginner needs in a horse.
Vicarious means experienced secondhand, which does not fit.

definition: causing great harm, often in a gradual way that is not easily noticed

examples.text: The pernicious weed spread through the wetland before anyone noticed it.
The pamphlet warned of the pernicious influence of bribery on the courts.
The pernicious habit of checking my phone at night was wrecking my sleep.

confused.note: Pernicious means harmful; pernickety means fussy about small details.

questions.passage: The rumor seemed too silly to matter, but its effects were ______. Over several months it slowly eroded customers' trust in the bank, and by the time managers responded, a third of the deposits had been withdrawn.
questions.explanation: Slowly eroding trust until deposits fled is gradual, serious harm.

distractors.why: Benign means harmless, which is how the rumor wrongly seemed.
Lavish means rich and generous, which does not describe harm.
Apocryphal means of doubtful truth; that might describe the rumor, not its effects.

definition: changing mood or opinion quickly and unpredictably

examples.text: The mercurial duke rewards a jester at noon and exiles him by nightfall.
The mercurial queen changed ministers four times in a single year.
My mercurial little brother can go from giggles to tears in ten seconds.

confused.note: Mercurial means quick to change; mercenary means motivated only by money.

questions.passage: Working for the director required patience, for her temperament was ______. A scene she had praised as perfect in the morning might, by afternoon, strike her as an embarrassment that had to be reshot at once.
questions.explanation: Praising a scene and then condemning it hours later shows quick, unpredictable changes.

distractors.why: Docile means calm and easily managed, the opposite of her temperament.
Pristine means unspoiled, which does not describe a temperament.
Compliant means willing to go along, which she was not.

partsNote: from Mercury, the swift messenger god, and the quick-moving metal

definition: having little energy; slow and sleepy

examples.text: Reptiles become lethargic when the temperature drops.
The lethargic town stirs only when the weekly train arrives.
I feel lethargic after a big lunch and need a walk to wake up.

confused.note: Lethargic means sluggish; lethal means deadly.

questions.passage: Zookeepers knew something was wrong when the normally playful otter became ______. It stopped chasing its companions, ignored its favorite fish, and spent most of the day lying motionless on a rock.
questions.explanation: Lying motionless and ignoring food show a lack of energy.

distractors.why: Vigilant means alert and watchful, which the otter was not.
Tenacious means persistent, which does not describe a listless animal.
Obsequious means fawning, which does not fit.

definition: to cause something to start, especially something bad

examples.text: Agents were sent to instigate a revolt in the border provinces.
The jealous cousin instigates the quarrel and then pretends to be shocked by it.
My sister instigated the pillow fight and then blamed me.

confused.note: Instigate means to start or stir up; investigate means to look into.

questions.passage: The inquiry sought to learn who had ______ the riot. Witnesses agreed that the crowd had been calm until a small group at the back began throwing bottles and urging others to storm the gates.
questions.explanation: Throwing bottles and urging others on is starting the trouble.

distractors.why: Quelled means put down or calmed, the opposite of starting a riot.
Investigated means examined; the inquiry investigates, but the group started the riot.
Flouted means openly disobeyed a rule, which does not fit "the riot."

partsNote: from Latin stigare, "to prick, to urge"

definition: living alone and avoiding other people

examples.text: The reclusive poet published nothing in her lifetime and rarely left her room.
The reclusive spider hides in woodpiles and bites only when pressed.
Our reclusive neighbor waves from the window but never comes to the block party.

confused.note: Reclusive means avoiding company; exclusive means limited to a select few.

questions.passage: After his third novel became a bestseller, the author grew increasingly ______. He moved to a farmhouse with no telephone, stopped answering letters, and was not photographed again for forty years.
questions.explanation: Moving away and cutting off contact is avoiding other people.

distractors.why: Gregarious means sociable, the opposite of his retreat.
Compliant means obedient, which is unrelated.
Lavish means extravagant, which a farmhouse without a telephone is not.

definition: a small amount of something, especially something good

examples.text: The treaty restored a modicum of order to the border.
Even the villain shows a modicum of pity for the orphan.
With a modicum of effort, the garage could actually fit a car.

confused.note: A modicum is a small amount; a medium is a middle size or a means of communication.

questions.passage: Anyone with a ______ of common sense, the judge remarked, would have realized that a stranger offering to double their money overnight was not to be trusted.
questions.explanation: Even a small amount of sense would have been enough.

distractors.why: A plethora is an excess, but the judge means even a little would do.
A debacle is a disastrous failure, which does not fit "of common sense."
A hiatus is a pause, which does not fit.

definition: to take power, a position, or rights by force or without the right to do so

examples.text: The king's brother usurped the throne while the heir was abroad.
The steward slowly usurps his master's authority until the servants obey only him.
The cat has usurped my favorite chair and shows no sign of leaving.

confused.note: To usurp is to seize power wrongfully; usury is lending money at unfairly high interest.

questions.passage: The constitution gives the power to declare war to the legislature alone. Critics charged that the president had ______ that power by ordering the invasion without a vote.
questions.explanation: Taking a power that belongs to another branch is seizing it without right.

distractors.why: Relinquished means gave up, the opposite of taking a power.
Fluctuated means rose and fell, which does not fit.
Instigated means started or provoked; one seizes a power, one does not provoke it.

definition: widely told as true but probably not true

examples.text: The story that the queen said "Let them eat cake" is almost certainly apocryphal.
The biographer repeats an apocryphal tale of the poet wrestling a bear.
The story about a classmate who slept through the SAT and still got a perfect score is apocryphal.

confused.note: Apocryphal means of doubtful truth; apocalyptic means relating to the end of the world.

questions.passage: Tour guides love to say that the architect was blinded so that he could never design a rival to the palace. The tale is ______: records show that he went on to build three more palaces and died wealthy at eighty.
questions.explanation: Records contradict the tale, so it is widely told but untrue.

distractors.why: Authentic means genuine, which the records disprove.
Pernicious means harmful, which is not the point being made about the tale.
Redundant means needlessly repeated, which does not address whether the tale is true.

definition: experienced by watching or reading about someone else, not by doing it yourself

examples.text: Readers get a vicarious thrill from the heroine's escape across the rooftops.
Crowds took vicarious pride in the explorer's return.
I get vicarious joy from watching cooking shows while eating cereal.

confused.note: Vicarious means experienced through another person; vivacious means lively.

questions.passage: He had never climbed anything higher than a ladder, yet he read every mountaineering memoir he could find. The books gave him a ______ sense of adventure, letting him feel the cold and the danger from the safety of his armchair.
questions.explanation: Feeling the adventure through others' accounts is experiencing it secondhand.

distractors.why: Futile means pointless, which does not describe the feeling the books gave him.
Subordinate means lower in rank, which does not fit.
Docile means easily managed, which does not fit.

definition: to openly refuse to obey a rule, law, or custom

examples.text: Smugglers flouted the embargo and grew rich.
The heroine flouts convention by traveling alone.
Drivers flout the speed limit on our street every single morning.

confused.note: To flout is to defy a rule openly; to flaunt is to show something off.

questions.passage: The city banned fireworks years ago, but many residents ______ the ban. On the holiday, rockets rise from nearly every rooftop while police, vastly outnumbered, look on.
questions.explanation: Setting off fireworks openly despite the ban is defying it.

distractors.why: Flaunt means to show off; a ban is flouted, not flaunted.
Usurp means to seize power wrongfully, which is not what residents do to a ban.
Instigate means to start or stir up, which does not fit ignoring a ban.

definition: too eager to please or obey someone important

examples.text: The obsequious waiter laughs at every one of the banker's jokes.
Obsequious courtiers assured the king that the war was going well.
His obsequious emails to the teacher always begin "Your brilliant lecture today."

confused.note: Obsequious means fawning; obstreperous means noisy and hard to control.

questions.passage: The new assistant's manner struck his colleagues as ______. He rushed to open doors for the director, praised her most ordinary remarks as "inspired," and agreed with whatever she had said last.
questions.explanation: Rushing to flatter and agree with the boss is excessive eagerness to please.

distractors.why: Impartial means unbiased, which constant flattery is not.
Reclusive means avoiding people, but he sought out the director.
Tenacious means persistent, which is not the quality his colleagues noticed.

definition: to move or be shaped like waves, rising and falling gently

examples.text: The eel undulates its whole body to swim.
Fields of wheat undulate in the wind like a golden sea.
The road undulates over a dozen small hills before reaching the coast.

confused.note: To undulate is to move in smooth waves; to fluctuate is to change up and down irregularly.

questions.passage: Seen from the air, the dunes ______ toward the horizon in long, smooth ridges, each rising gently and then sinking again like a swell on a calm sea.
questions.explanation: Ridges that rise and sink like swells have a wavelike shape.

distractors.why: Fluctuate means to change irregularly over time; the dunes have a wave shape, they are not changing.
Usurp means to seize wrongfully, which does not fit.
Flout means to defy a rule, which does not fit.
